issues.legal_issue: An agreement to sell a publicly allotted residential site is unenforceable when its terms defeat the statutory scheme governing the allotment.
material_facts: A public authority allotted a site to a person under rules requiring the allottee to construct a residential building and restricting alienation.
The allottee agreed to sell the vacant site, deliver possession to the buyer, and convey title after obtaining the authority’s sale deed.
The agreement fixed consideration for the site alone and left no practical possibility for the allottee to fulfil the obligation to construct a residential building.
The buyer sought specific performance of that agreement.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was unlawful and unenforceable because enforcing it would defeat the statutory rules governing the public allotment.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 10 and 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 require a lawful object and render void an agreement whose object is forbidden by law or would defeat the provisions of law. Statutory rules are law for this purpose. Under Rules 17 and 18 of the City of Bangalore Improvement (Allotment of Sites) Rules, 1972, an allottee was required to build a residential building, and a vacant site could not simply be sold to a third party in the circumstances presented. Section 29(3) of the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945 gave restrictions in a grant or transfer effect according to their terms. Applying Kedar Nath Motani v. Prahlad Rai, AIR 1960 SC 213, and Narayanamma v. Govindappa, (2019) 19 SCC 42, the Court considered whether the illegality went to the root of the claim and whether the claimant had to rely on it. Jambu Rao Satappa Kocheri v. Neminath Appayya Hanamannayar, AIR 1968 SC 1358, and the conditional-decree cases including Motilal v. Nanhelal, AIR 1930 PC 287, were distinguished: those cases concerned contracts capable of lawful completion after permission or fulfilment of a condition, unlike this agreement, which defeated the allotment scheme itself.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and public_residential_allotment and allottee_required_to_build and agreement_requires_vacant_site_transfer and agreement_prevents_required_construction and claim_depends_on_agreement

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.public_residential_allotment: A public authority allotted the property under a scheme intended to provide sites for residential construction.
predicates.allottee_required_to_build: The allottee was required to construct a residential building on the allotted site.
predicates.agreement_requires_vacant_site_transfer: The agreement contemplated transfer of the vacant site rather than transfer of a site with the required building.
predicates.agreement_prevents_required_construction: The agreement’s terms prevented or made practically impossible the allottee’s required construction.
predicates.claim_depends_on_agreement: The claimant’s case for relief depended on enforcing that agreement.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claim depends on an agreement that prevents an allottee from fulfilling a required residential-construction obligation under a public allotment scheme, specific performance is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of lis pendens applies to a transfer of property during litigation only when the transfer is made by a party to that litigation.
material_facts: A suit concerning the property was pending when the son of the original allottee transferred the property to a purchaser.
The son and the purchaser were not parties to the suit when the transfer took place and were impleaded later.
The allottee’s husband was already a party and had given a no-objection that enabled the son to obtain title.

The Court held that even if the husband’s conduct could be treated as dealing with the property, lis pendens would not invalidate the later sale; at most, a transfer by a party would remain subject to the final result of the litigation.
issues.conclusion: The sale by the son was not hit by lis pendens because he was not a party to the suit when he made the transfer. The High Court erred in holding otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the doctrine of lis pendens. Its indispensable requirement is that the transfer or other dealing with the property be made by a party to the litigation while the proceeding is pending. The doctrine is based on expediency and the finality of adjudication, not notice or good faith. A transfer to which the doctrine applies is not void; it is subject to the final decision. The Court relied on the principle expressed in pendente lite nihil innovetur and considered the treatment of the doctrine in Manjeshwara Krishnaya v. Vasudeva Mallya, AIR 1918 Mad 578, and distinguished Nallakumara Goundan v. Pappayi Ammal, AIR 1945 Mad 219.

predicates.property_in_litigation: The property being transferred was the subject matter of a pending proceeding.
predicates.transfer_during_pending_proceeding: The transfer took place while that proceeding was pending.
predicates.transferor_not_party: The person who made the transfer was not a party to the proceeding at the time of transfer.

issues.definition: A transfer made during a proceeding is not hit by lis pendens when the transferred property is in litigation but the transferor is not a party to that proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer supported by a sale deed is not a sham merely because the purchaser may not have acted in good faith.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that the purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser and that the sale was intended to complicate the dispute.
The amended pleading did not allege that the sale deed was a sham transaction.
The sale deed was executed in favour of the purchaser, and the Court distinguished a sham transaction, which conveys no title, from a transaction in which the purchaser’s good faith is disputed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in characterising the sale as a sham transaction; the sale deed conveyed title, and the alleged absence of bona fides was a distinct issue.
issues.legal_principle: A sham transaction and a sale that is not bona fide are different: a sham transaction conveys no title, whereas a non-bona-fide purchaser may still acquire title. The Court considered the distinction between a sham transaction and the bona-fide-purchaser question arising under Section 19(1)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

predicates.sale_deed_executed: A sale deed was executed in favour of the purchaser.
predicates.sham_transaction_not_pleaded: The claimant did not plead that the transaction was a sham.
predicates.only_purchaser_good_faith_disputed: The dispute concerned the purchaser’s good faith rather than whether the parties intended any sale at all.

issues.definition: When a sale deed was executed and the pleadings dispute only the purchaser’s good faith, the sale is not a sham on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s lack of bona fides does not entitle a claimant to specific performance of an agreement that is itself unenforceable.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied on an agreement that the Court held unlawful and unenforceable.
The High Court had found that the subsequent purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
The Court concluded that, even assuming that finding was correct, it could not assist the plaintiff because the plaintiff’s claim depended on the unenforceable agreement.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser’s alleged lack of bona fides did not advance the plaintiff’s claim, and specific performance remained unavailable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(1)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes the status of a subsequent purchaser relevant to enforcement of a specific-performance decree. That protection cannot supply an enforceable contract where the agreement itself is unlawful. Applying the principles in Kedar Nath Motani v. Prahlad Rai, AIR 1960 SC 213, and Narayanamma v. Govindappa, (2019) 19 SCC 42, the Court held that the plaintiff could not obtain the Court’s assistance to enforce an agreement that depended on an illegality going to the root of the claim.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.agreement_unenforceable: The agreement on which the claim depended was held unenforceable.
predicates.purchaser_good_faith_disputed: The parties disputed whether a subsequent purchaser acted in good faith.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, a dispute about a subsequent purchaser’s good faith does not make specific performance available when the underlying agreement is unenforceable.

issues.legal_issue: The Court may grant monetary relief in place of specific performance to do complete justice when the agreement cannot be enforced.
material_facts: The plaintiff had paid the agreed consideration under the unenforceable agreement.
The Trial Court had ordered repayment of the amount paid, while the High Court had ordered conveyance of the property.
The property’s substantial value and the amount paid were before the Court, as were the parties’ conduct and the evidence concerning the transaction.
The Court allowed the appeals, dismissed the specific-performance suit, and ordered a larger monetary payment to the plaintiff’s legal representatives.
issues.conclusion: The specific-performance suit was dismissed, but the appellants were ordered to pay the plaintiff’s legal representatives a sum of money to do complete justice between the parties.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution of India empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice between the parties. In exercising that power, the Court considered the evidence, the parties’ conduct, the payment made under the agreement, and the value of the property. The Court also considered the nature of its jurisdiction under Article 136.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and specific_performance_refused and payment_made_under_agreement and circumstances_support_complete_justice_relief

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter came before the Supreme Court in an appeal.
predicates.specific_performance_refused: The Court refused to order specific performance.
predicates.payment_made_under_agreement: The claimant had paid money under the agreement that could not be enforced.
predicates.circumstances_support_complete_justice_r: The evidence and circumstances led the Court to grant monetary relief to achieve complete justice.

issues.definition: When the Supreme Court refuses specific performance, money was paid under the agreement, and the circumstances support complete-justice relief, the Court may award monetary relief instead.
